AsDB reiterates that the negative override clause in AsDB’s Access to Information Policy can only be exercised in exceptional circumstances, upon approval of the Board of Directors. This represents the highest approving authority in ADB, further emphasizing that the negative override clause is not to be used lightly. 

Further, since the presence of a negative override clause is already effectively penalized in scoring “limitations on commercially sensitive information and sensitive internal deliberations information” (e.g., including cases where its counterparty may veto the classification or release of sensitive information, which can be a basis of exercising a negative override), it should no longer be considered unfavorably as well on the “presumption of disclosure” part of the criteria. Moreover, a negative override is a standard feature of access to information policies—again, as a provision for exceptional circumstances—so it seems that adopting a stringent view on the mere presence of a negative override will render institutions with such policies essentially unable to meet the first and second parts of the scoring criteria.

Thank you for this feedback.

The presence of a negative override undermines the presumption of disclosure since it can be employed at the discretion of the institution. The policy already protects interests against harm through the named exceptions, so any information that falls into the scope of those can simply be withheld by applying these regular exceptions. The negative override falls outside the named exceptions which is why it is not penalised under that criterion of the test and is viewed as undermining the presumption of disclosure. The presumption of disclosure  should apply in all cases except those that fall under the named exceptions. 

Please note that we have applied the same approach to all other institutions whose policies include a negative override. This applies to some development banks while some do not have such a mechanism in their policy.

While it's obvious  it's not bank's intention to use the negative override clause lightly (only in exceptional circumstances and with the Board approval), I agree that it undermines presumption of disclosure as it is within bank's power to decide when to use it.

Publish What You Fund completed an assessment of the quality of disclosure policies based on the overarching approach taken in the Global Right to Information Rating. The scoring system is a cumulative measure of 3 key indicators: 1/presumption of disclosure, 2/Limitations on commercially sensitive information and sensitive internal deliberations information, and 3/ independent appeals process. 1. presumption of disclosure- YES (5) 2. Limitations on commercially sensitive information and sensitive internal deliberations information. To score on this indicator, non-disclosure clauses related to these matters must (a) clearly define a legitimate interest that is being protected, (b) be limited to protecting that interest against harm, and (c) be subject to a public interest override. The Gates Foundation Information Sharing Approach lists disclosure exceptions/limitations. Several of these identify the interest being protected from harm (safety, privacy etc.), however for internal deliberations the reference to “sensitive internal deliberations information” does not pass our three part test (see above, taken from the 2022 Index methodology paper). Instead, the policy should identify the specific interests which are being protected here. Normally, these would be interests (along with harm tests) such as: • Frustrating the success of a policy, by premature disclosure of that policy (in the policy this applies to documents but is not specified for deliberations) • Undermining the deliberative process within the organisation by inhibiting the free and frank provision of advice or exchange of views. • Significantly undermining the effectiveness of a testing or auditing procedure used by the organisation. • Causing serious prejudice to an ongoing investigation by the organisation. Neither could we could not find a public interest override for the exceptions. 3. independent appeals Yes - appeals process found: https://secure.ethicspoint.com/domain/media/en/gui/7589/index.html - ability to select an 'other' country

1. Presumption of disclosure: YES
2. Limited exceptions: NO. Following the review of EIB's Group Transparency Policy the following language was added to the policy: 

"5.5 Access to information/documents shall also be refused where disclosure would undermine the protection of commercial interests of a natural or legal person. The following non-exhaustive examples illustrate common cases of commercial interests: 
o Business, financial, proprietary or other non-public information/documents created or received by the EIB; 
o Information/documents relating to negotiations, legal documentation and related correspondence; 
o Information/documents covered by a confidentiality agreement or in relation to which a third party has legitimate expectations that they would not be disclosed."

This does not meet the criterion of limited exceptions we use to assess this indicator. Firstly, these examples are not interests, rather they are types of document/information. For exceptions relating to commercially sensitive information we would expect the policy to clearly define the legitimate interest being protected and for the exception to be limited to protecting that interest against harm. Second, allowing a confidentiality agreement or the expectation of a third party to invoke non-disclosure undermines the limited approach to exceptions. In both of these cases there is no requirement to subject information disclosure to an objective test for harm of legitimate interests.

3. Independent Appeals Process: YES - European Ombudsman

Article 5.5. of the EIB Transparency Policy (EIB-TP), in its new formulation, is composed by two parts. The first subparagraph sets out the content of the exception (i.e. disclosure shall be refused when disclosure would undermine the commercial interest of a natural or legal person). The second subparagraph illustrates, with some non-exhaustive examples, cases where the disclosure of the information covered by the exception could possibly harm commercial interests. 

Such examples refer to situations that are common in banking, and as such they help parties that are not transparency experts (or may be more familiar with the legal framework applicable to public authorities access to documents) to better understand the exception under article 5.5, and how it can apply to some of the activities of the EIB. 

The second subparagraph is thus intended to illustrate, but not to modify, the commercial interest exception. In other words, it does not mean that the EIB in principle does not disclose the mentioned types of documents/information upon request. 

Following a disclosure request, the EIB analyses relevant documents/information individually in order to determine whether their disclosure would harm legitimate interests. The EIB also considers whether there is a public interest in disclosure, which would prevail over the protection of commercial interests. The EIB explains its decision in answer to each disclosure request.

In particular, the application of the exception continues to be subject to:
o	Article 5.8, according to which the commercial interest exception (and other relevant exceptions) applies unless there is an overriding public interest in disclosure. Where an overriding public interest exists (e.g. in the case of information relating to emissions into the environment), the commercial interests exception may not be applied. 
o	Article 5.9, according to which the grounds for refusal, in particular as regards access to environmental information and documents, should be interpreted in a restrictive way. This provision forbids an unduly broad interpretation of disclosure exceptions, including the commercial interest exception.

We assess the policy on the basis of its content. If the examples given are cases where the disclosure of the information covered by the exception could possibly harm commercial interests, they should be referred to as such. 

The policy can currently be interpreted as allowing a confidentiality agreement or the expectation of a third party to invoke non-disclosure and as such it does not meet our criteria under criterion 2 of this indicator.

1. Presumption of disclosure: YES
2. Limited exceptions: NO. Following the review of EIB's Group Transparency Policy the following language was added to the policy: 5.5 Access to information/documents shall also be refused where disclosure would undermine the protection of commercial interests of a natural or legal person. The following non-exhaustive examples illustrate common cases of commercial interests: o Business, financial, proprietary or other non-public information/documents created or received by the EIB; o Information/documents relating to negotiations, legal documentation and related correspondence; o Information/documents covered by a confidentiality agreement or in relation to which a third party has legitimate expectations that they would not be disclosed. This does not meet the criterion of limited exceptions we use to assess this indicator. Firstly, these examples are not interests, rather they are types of document/information. For exceptions relating to commercially sensitive information we would expect the policy to clearly define the legitimate interest being protected and for the exception to be limited to protecting that interest against harm. Second, allowing a confidentiality agreement or the expectation of a third party to invoke non-disclosure undermines the limited approach to exceptions. In both of these cases there is no requirement to subject information disclosure to an objective test for harm of legitimate interests.
3. Independent Appeals Process: YES - European Ombudsman

Article 5.5. of the EIB Transparency Policy (EIB-TP), in its new formulation, is composed by two parts. The first subparagraph sets out the content of the exception (i.e. disclosure shall be refused when disclosure would undermine the commercial interest of a natural or legal person). The second subparagraph illustrates, with some non-exhaustive examples, cases where the disclosure of the information covered by the exception could possibly harm commercial interests. 

Such examples refer to situations that are common in banking, and as such they help parties that are not transparency experts (or may be more familiar with the legal framework applicable to public authorities access to documents) to better understand the exception under article 5.5, and how it can apply to some of the activities of the EIB. 

The second subparagraph is thus intended to illustrate, but not to modify, the commercial interest exception. In other words, it does not mean that the EIB in principle does not disclose the mentioned types of documents/information upon request. 

Following a disclosure request, the EIB analyses relevant documents/information individually in order to determine whether their disclosure would harm legitimate interests. The EIB also considers whether there is a public interest in disclosure, which would prevail over the protection of commercial interests. The EIB explains its decision in answer to each disclosure request.

In particular, the application of the exception continues to be subject to:
o	Article 5.8, according to which the commercial interest exception (and other relevant exceptions) applies unless there is an overriding public interest in disclosure. Where an overriding public interest exists (e.g. in the case of information relating to emissions into the environment), the commercial interests exception may not be applied. 
o	Article 5.9, according to which the grounds for refusal, in particular as regards access to environmental information and documents, should be interpreted in a restrictive way. This provision forbids an unduly broad interpretation of disclosure exceptions, including the commercial interest exception.

We assess the policy on the basis of its content. If the examples given are cases where the disclosure of the information covered by the exception could possibly harm commercial interests, they should be referred to as such. 

The policy can currently be interpreted as allowing a confidentiality agreement or the expectation of a third party to invoke non-disclosure and as such it does not meet our criteria under criterion 2 of this indicator.

We thank PWYF for granting us full scores for the presumption of disclosure and independent review mechanism aspects of this indicator. We are still not satisfied with PWYF's assessment on the second element of the test, limited exceptions. According to the methodology adopted by PWYF this element includes three specific components: (A) clear identification of a legitimate interest being protected; (B) restriction is limited to protecting such interest against harm; and (C) there is a positive override for public interest. There is no dispute that IDB Invest policy includes a positive override (paragraphs 62 and 63), so we focus our comments in the first two aspects. For each of the exceptions included the IDB Invest Access to Information Policy, the policy explicitly indicates the legitimate interest being protected. For example, for the “commercially sensitive exception” the policy states that it covers: “commercial, proprietary, financial, privileged, intellectual property, or other non-public information about its clients, co-financiers, investors, or third parties. To do so would be contrary to the legitimate expectations of such parties, who need to be able to communicate detailed information to IDB Invest without fear of compromising confidential information.” For the “deliberative information exception” the policy states “information that would affect the integrity of the decision-making process or inhibit the free and candid exchange of ideas in the deliberative processes. By protecting this information based on its function and content, IDB Invest seeks to safeguard a space for reflection and discussion free of public scrutiny”, and so forth. In other words, the policy does identify the legitimate interest being protected in each case, and paragraphs 11 and 51 explicitly require that there is harm to the protected interest to configurate the exception. In the second review PWYF insists on focusing on an element (not included in the methodology) concerning the process of determination of confidentiality and the role of third parties in the process. Firstly, while IDB Invest respects and values the advocacy role of PWYF, we consider that the Aid Transparency Index should be assessed based strictly on the methodology disseminated, and not on other criteria. And secondly, IDB Invest handles information of third parties, and those third parties must be consulted in the process of making the assessment of confidentiality of the information provided by them (this is of the essence of the business model of private sector financing, so we don’t see how this could be penalized). PWYF extracts the wrong conclusion when it assumes that this consultation precluded IDB Invest from making an autonomous judgement. In fact, PWYF can read the files of all cases brought before IDB Invest review mechanism and you would notice that there is not a single case in which the decision of withholding information is based on a third party’s assertion of confidentiality.

What is the specific language of a negative override? We do not consider this a negative override, and others have considered adopting this language in their policies believing it doesn't represent a negative override. Please confirm which third parties are exempted? Not sure what this means.

Negative override: 
The language is in article 10 of the policy - “10. There is a presumption in favor of disclosure with respect to the information described in paragraph 8 above, absent a compelling reason not to disclose such information. In determining whether any particular information is to be made available by IFC as a routine matter or upon request, IFC first considers whether such information falls within the scope of IFC’s responsibilities in paragraph 8 and, if so, then determines whether there is any compelling reason not to disclose all or any part of such information. In making this determination, IFC considers whether the disclosure of information is likely to cause harm to specific parties or interests that outweighs the benefit of disclosure or whether the information contains or makes reference to information described in the list of exceptions below, which are not exhaustive.” 

This language undermines the principle of presumed disclosure limited by named exceptions (our first criterion) - the article indicates that there is another determination process outside the named exceptions that can restrict access to information without reference to the exceptions. 

Criterion 2 on limited exceptions fails our assessment because of article 11.(a). This sets out the exception on commercially sensitive and confidential information. This information is restricted based on it being provided as confidential information, meaning the third party decides on confidentiality. It does not identify specific legitimate harms or apply a harm test for decisions to restrict information.

Unlike other bilateral or Multilateral organizations which operate through a project-based model (i.e., where funds are strictly associated with specific projects) UNICEF operates through a results-based model, more similar to that of a private company that must regularly assess how far they are from achieving their goals and redirect their efforts to fulfill them. The result-based model works in 4 levels: Country Programme, Outcomes, Outputs and Activities.  UNICEF outputs are published to IATI schema as IATI-Activities. As defined in our Strategic Plan UNICEF has identified 9 overarching change strategies as key to accelerating progress towards achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals and realizing children’s rights. - Regarding the openness presumption: 

1.	Regarding the openness presumption, the "Principle 1: Maximize access to information" of the current IDB's Access to Information Policy, set in section 2.1, reaffirms the Bank's commitment to transparency in all its activities seeking to maximize access to any documents and information that it produces and to information in its possession that is not on the list of exceptions. In this regard, the standard of disclosure set in section 3.1 of the IDB Policy Framework is that "The Bank seeks to maximize access to information that it produces and will therefore disclose any information not contained on a list of exceptions. The policy is predicated not on a list of information it chooses to disclose but on a clear definition of information it will not disclose."

2.	Additionally, regarding the project documents, the Implementation Guidelines of the current IDB's Access to Information Policy states that the "Bank operates under a presumption in favor of public Disclosure of Information and will disclose any information not contained on a list of exceptions." 

3.	On the other hand, Section 8 of the IDB ATI Policy related to "Overrides" sets the Bank's prerogative to provide access to certain specified types of information ordinarily subject to one of the policy's exceptions. Similarly, the Bank could exclude commonly available information from access based on the premise that access would occasion more harm than benefit, requiring the Committee's express written authorization. In both circumstances, the positive and negative override will require the allegation of extraordinary cases, and the IDB Access to Information Committee's decision on this regard, especially for the "Negative Override," shall be adopted "based on the premise that access would occasion more harm than benefit."

4.	Therefore, the Openness Presumption in the policy is protected under the above requirements set in the IDB Access to Information Framework (Policy and Implementation Guidelines) to apply any negative override decision, which strengthens the maximization of access to information as the standard of disclosure and as a default rule for the disclosure of the information in possession of the Bank.

- Regarding the criterion "Contains exceptions with public interest over-ride":   

The positive override is included in section 8 of the Access to Information Policy based on the determination made by the Bank that “the benefit to be derived from doing so would outweigh the potential harm that application of the policy might otherwise entail.”

On the other hand, the IDB ATI Policy exceptions have been drafted considering the ownership of the information following international trends on this matter. Therefore, if the ownership of the information belongs to a third party, the latter is entitled to express their interest in being affected by the disclosure. It is important that all legitimate interests are adequately balanced, otherwise the Bank could disclose information even though this may cause unwarranted harm.

Please refer to the email "2024 Aid Transparency Index, Access to Information Policy scoring" sent to IDB on 09/10/2023. To quote from the email: 

"While one of the sub-criteria for 'limitations of commercially sensitive information and internal deliberations information' is that a positive public interest override should be in place, we have found that many policies also include a negative override, sometimes also referred to as a prerogative to restrict access to information. These clauses allow a discretionary power to the organisation to restrict access to information, bypassing the usual named exceptions for information disclosure. 

Our research has concluded that the presence of a negative override/prerogative to restrict access to information undermines the presumption of disclosure contained in a policy. On this basis we will be scoring down those policies that contain such a clause for the presumption of disclosure criterion for the indicator.

In the case of IDB we identified the presence of a negative override in the current policy but this appears to have been removed in the proposed new policy. If your policy is updated before the final Aid Transparency Index assessment in early April 2024, please do let us know."

Regarding criterion 2 - limited exceptions - where a third party can determine whether information is disclosed this does not meet the threshold for this criterion. Harms must be identified and non-disclosure limited to protection of that harm. Where a third party can decide on disclosure this bypasses the harm test and so does not meet the criterion.

Please clarify the decreased score here. There have been no substantive changes to DevTracker since ATI22, where FCDO scored full marks for Accessibility. The indicator definition also remains the same for both ATI22 and ATI24. IATI data for individual programmes can be downloaded directly from the DevTracker. Furthermore, bulk downloads are available via the Solr API for DevTracker, with users able to amend the parameters according to their search preferences.

This change is due to the fact that the ‘bulk download’ option has gone from DevTracker (something other agencies have noted when using DevTracker as well). No alternate API function found on Devtracker. 
Note that raw IATI files are not accepted for this indicator as the underlying principle behind it is to assess what organisations are doing to promote access and use of their aid information. Information published to the IATI Registry is taken into account for the publication indicators.

FCDO have addedd bulk download section on the 'about' page :

'In addition, summary data for all FCDO programmes collectively is available in CSV format detailing the title, description, budget, location and start and end dates - this data is published under the Open Government Licence v3.0. '

As discussed with PWYF, there was previously no change in functionality within DevTracker. However, we have taken on board this feedback and since added a brand new bulk download feature for FCDO programmes. This feature is available via the ‘About Us’ page on DevTracker [https://devtracker.fcdo.gov.uk/about] under a new section called ‘How can I download the data in Development Tracker?’. The link provides users with data from FCDO’s own API which covers the following indicators for all FCDO programmes (open and closed) in CVS format: IATI ID, Title, Description, Budget, Location, Stand and end dates (including planned and actual). Specifically, this provides free, bulk export of data containing detailed disaggregated data which is published under an open licence. The data source is via our own aid portal and covers all published activities in the countries and sectors in which FCDO operates with more than five activity-level indicators including financial information.
